1.pericope_label: Then said Solomon, The Lord hath said that he would dwell in the thick darkness. But I have built an house of habitation for thee, and a place for thy dwelling for ever. And the king turned his face, and blessed the whole congregation of Israel: and all the congregation of Israel stood. And he said, Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who hath with his hands fulfilled that which he spake with his mouth to my father David, saying, Since the day that I brought forth my people out of the land of Egypt I chose no city among all the tribes of Israel to build an house in, that my name might be there; neither chose I any man to be a ruler over my people Israel: But I have chosen Jerusalem, that my name might be there; and have chosen David to be over my people Israel.

schools.summary: Ellicott reads these verses as a textual critic working beside the parallel account: he restores the emphasis of the opening claim, prefers the doubled verb of the older book as original, marks two words of the dedication formula as poetic and judges an inserted conjunction to weaken the parallelism, notes a singular against a plural whose unpointed Hebrew could be read either way, and defends the clause about God choosing no ruler as possibly belonging to the older text from the first — drawing from it the remark that Scripture nowhere teaches the voice of the people to be the voice of God.

Henry opens on motive rather than masonry, holding that it matters greatly in religious action that the eye be single, and sets out the king's three inducements: the glory of God, who has made darkness his pavilion toward us while dwelling in unapproachable light; the prior choice of the city, which makes it fit that the house raised for God should excel the buildings raised for men; and the carrying out of a father's intention never fulfilled.

themes: Then said Solomon, The Lord hath said that he would dwell in the thick darkness.
But I have built an house of habitation for thee, and a place for thy dwelling for ever.

But I have chosen Jerusalem, that my name might be there; and have chosen David to be over my people Israel.

9.pericope_label: Notwithstanding thou shalt not build the house; but thy son which shall come forth out of thy loins, he shall build the house for my name. The Lord therefore hath performed his word that he hath spoken: for I am risen up in the room of David my father, and am set on the throne of Israel, as the Lord promised, and have built the house for the name of the Lord God of Israel. And in it have I put the ark, wherein is the covenant of the Lord, that he made with the children of Israel. And he stood before the altar of the Lord in the presence of all the congregation of Israel, and spread forth his hands: For Solomon had made a brasen scaffold, of five cubits long, and five cubits broad, and three cubits high, and had set it in the midst of the court: and upon it he stood, and kneeled down upon his knees before all the congregation of Israel, and spread forth his hands toward heaven, And said, O Lord God of Israel, there is no God like thee in the heaven, nor in the earth; which keepest covenant, and shewest mercy unto thy servants, that walk before thee with all their hearts:

schools.summary: Ellicott hears the stress fall on the pronoun in the refusal to David, renders the establishing of the promise literally as causing it to rise up, records the abridgement by which a place for the ark becomes the ark itself, and gives the fullest attention to the platform of prayer — a verse absent from the parallel that may once have stood there, describing a structure like a laver turned upside down, with kneeling and outspread hands an attitude figured on Egyptian monuments; on the opening address he finds the Syriac a curious echo of the Lord's Prayer and reads covenant and mercy as one idea.

Wesley turns the refusal outward — one sows and another reaps, and let no man think it a disparagement to pursue the good designs of those before him — and reads the prayer as making the temple a figure of Christ the Mediator; Clarke supplies the Targum's expansion of walking before God with the whole heart, as all the will of the soul and all the affection of the heart.

Henry marks the moment the deed of dedication gives way to the consecration-prayer, and gathers the doctrine the prayer assumes: that God is of incomparable perfection, having no peer as every creature has its fellow; that he is true to every word, so that those who walk before him with all their hearts find him as good as his word and better; that he is infinite, the heaven of heavens unable to contain him and nothing added to his blessedness by our service; and that he alone knows the hearts of men.

themes: Notwithstanding thou shalt not build the house; but thy son which shall come forth out of thy loins, he shall build the house for my name.

16.pericope_label: Now therefore, O Lord God of Israel, keep with thy servant David my father that which thou hast promised him, saying, There shall not fail thee a man in my sight to sit upon the throne of Israel; yet so that thy children take heed to their way to walk in my law, as thou hast walked before me. Now then, O Lord God of Israel, let thy word be verified, which thou hast spoken unto thy servant David. But will God in very deed dwell with men on the earth? behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house which I have built! Have respect therefore to the prayer of thy servant, and to his supplication, O Lord my God, to hearken unto the cry and the prayer which thy servant prayeth before thee:

schools.summary: Ellicott follows the turn from thanksgiving to petition word by word: the further promise distinguished from the one already fulfilled, the condition tightened from yet so that to only if, the single departure from the parallel explained as the chronicler avoiding a seeming tautology, and the great question about God dwelling with men traced through the Greek and Latin, which render it as asking whether such a thing is credible at all.

Clarke gives the Targum's expansion of that question in full — who could have imagined, who could have thought it credible, that God should place his majesty among men on earth, when the highest heavens cannot bear the glory of that majesty, nor can this house contain him.

themes: Now therefore, O Lord God of Israel, keep with thy servant David my father that which thou hast promised him, saying, There shall not fail thee a man in my sight to sit upon the throne of Israel; yet so that thy children take heed to their way to walk in my law, as thou hast walked before me.

20.pericope_label: That thine eyes may be open upon this house day and night, upon the place whereof thou hast said that thou wouldest put thy name there; to hearken unto the prayer which thy servant prayeth toward this place. Hearken therefore unto the supplications of thy servant, and of thy people Israel, which they shall make toward this place: hear thou from thy dwelling place, even from heaven; and when thou hearest, forgive. If a man sin against his neighbour, and an oath be laid upon him to make him swear, and the oath come before thine altar in this house; Then hear thou from heaven, and do, and judge thy servants, by requiting the wicked, by recompensing his way upon his own head; and by justifying the righteous, by giving him according to his righteousness. And if thy people Israel be put to the worse before the enemy, because they have sinned against thee; and shall return and confess thy name, and pray and make supplication before thee in this house;

schools.summary: Ellicott keeps returning to the house as a direction rather than a dwelling, noting that where this text says hear from, the parallel says unto, a compressed construction he judges original; he states without embarrassment that the temple was and remains the point toward which a Jew turns to pray, rejects the marginal reading that would obscure it, marks the word for supplications as poetic and late, and in the clause about requital prefers the parallel's find guilty because it balances the justifying of a just man.

Wesley draws out what the petitions assume about prayer, that Solomon asks not for help without praying but for help in answer to prayer, and that even the intercession of Christ does not supersede our supplications but encourages them; Clarke points his reader to his own treatment of the seven cases in the parallel chapter.

themes: That thine eyes may be open upon this house day and night, upon the place whereof thou hast said that thou wouldest put thy name there; to hearken unto the prayer which thy servant prayeth toward this place.

27.pericope_label: Then hear thou from heaven, and forgive the sin of thy servants, and of thy people Israel, when thou hast taught them the good way, wherein they should walk; and send rain upon thy land, which thou hast given unto thy people for an inheritance. If there be dearth in the land, if there be pestilence, if there be blasting, or mildew, locusts, or caterpillers; if their enemies besiege them in the cities of their land; whatsoever sore or whatsoever sickness there be: Then what prayer or what supplication soever shall be made of any man, or of all thy people Israel, when every one shall know his own sore and his own grief, and shall spread forth his hands in this house: Then hear thou from heaven thy dwelling place, and forgive, and render unto every man according unto all his ways, whose heart thou knowest; (for thou only knowest the hearts of the children of men:)

schools.summary: Ellicott, the only witness the catena supplies here, works the passage as a scholar with two manuscripts open: he would read the appeal as to or in heaven rather than from it, suspects a miscopied particle in the clause about teaching the good way, sets out what the ancient versions made of the strange phrase in the land of his gates, judges the doubled expression about a man's own sore and grief to be a gloss on the parallel's plague of his own heart, and notes both the distributive force of the article and a word dropped from the final clause.

themes: Then hear thou from heaven, and forgive the sin of thy servants, and of thy people Israel, when thou hast taught them the good way, wherein they should walk; and send rain upon thy land, which thou hast given unto thy people for an inheritance.

If there be dearth in the land, if there be pestilence, if there be blasting, or mildew, locusts, or caterpillers; if their enemies besiege them in the cities of their land; whatsoever sore or whatsoever sickness there be:

31.pericope_label: That they may fear thee, to walk in thy ways, so long as they live in the land which thou gavest unto our fathers. Moreover concerning the stranger, which is not of thy people Israel, but is come from a far country for thy great name’s sake, and thy mighty hand, and thy stretched out arm; if they come and pray in this house; Then hear thou from the heavens, even from thy dwelling place, and do according to all that the stranger calleth to thee for; that all people of the earth may know thy name, and fear thee, as doth thy people Israel, and may know that this house which I have built is called by thy name. If thy people go out to war against their enemies by the way that thou shalt send them, and they pray unto thee toward this city which thou hast chosen, and the house which I have built for thy name; Then hear thou from the heavens their prayer and their supplication, and maintain their cause.

schools.summary: Ellicott carries this section alone and tracks where the chronicler's hand shows: an explanatory phrase added about walking in God's ways, two verses of the older account apparently run together by a copyist so that the appeal to the great name arrives without its fuller clause, a plural he would restore in the word for peoples, a conjunction he would strike so that fearing becomes the purpose of knowing, the idiom of praying the way of a city, and the petition to accomplish the people's right, which the Latin sharpens into avenging them.

themes: That they may fear thee, to walk in thy ways, so long as they live in the land which thou gavest unto our fathers.

36.pericope_label: If they sin against thee, (for there is no man which sinneth not,) and thou be angry with them, and deliver them over before their enemies, and they carry them away captives unto a land far off or near; Yet if they bethink themselves in the land whither they are carried captive, and turn and pray unto thee in the land of their captivity, saying, We have sinned, we have done amiss, and have dealt wickedly; If they return to thee with all their heart and with all their soul in the land of their captivity, whither they have carried them captives, and pray toward their land, which thou gavest unto their fathers, and toward the city which thou hast chosen, and toward the house which I have built for thy name: Then hear thou from the heavens, even from thy dwelling place, their prayer and their supplications, and maintain their cause, and forgive thy people which have sinned against thee. Now, my God, let, I beseech thee, thine eyes be open, and let thine ears be attent unto the prayer that is made in this place.

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the confession as a climax rather than a repetition — we have slipped, we have done crookedly, we have been godless — finds the verse about the land of captivity uncertain and offers two ways out, distrusts a plural for supplications found nowhere else, and marks the decisive fact that from the plea for forgiveness onward the two accounts of the prayer are wholly dissimilar; his notes on that new material identify a word for attentive found besides only in one late psalm and a construction, the prayer of this place, occurring only here and in the answering passage.

Clarke points to his fuller treatment of the case in the parallel chapter and supplies the Targum's rendering of the turning-point, that the exiles bethink themselves when the fear of God returns into their hearts.

41.pericope_label: Now therefore arise, O Lord God, into thy resting place, thou, and the ark of thy strength: let thy priests, O Lord God, be clothed with salvation, and let thy saints rejoice in goodness. O Lord God, turn not away the face of thine anointed: remember the mercies of David thy servant.

schools.summary: Ellicott shows where the borrowed psalm has been altered — the added connective, a divine title absent from the older book and favoured by this writer, a late word for resting place where the psalm has the ordinary term, salvation standing where the psalm had righteousness, the transposed halves of a couplet reworked to introduce the mercies promised to David, and an imperative found only here and in Nehemiah — and judges that the idea of the sanctuary as God's resting place does not sit with the spirit of a prayer that has insisted the heaven of heavens cannot contain him.

Wesley reads the same petition in the opposite direction, paraphrasing it as a plea that God would arise from the throne of his glory and come down into the place appointed for his constant habitation, from which he will not remove; Clarke supplies Jarchi on both closing verses and notes the plain textual fact that these two verses are absent from the parallel account.

debates.question: Is the sanctuary God's resting place?

positions.position: The phrase is borrowed from a psalm and sits awkwardly in a prayer that has repeatedly said heaven cannot contain him.
It is the point the whole dedication has worked toward — that God would come down and make this place his constant habitation.

themes: Now therefore arise, O Lord God, into thy resting place, thou, and the ark of thy strength: let thy priests, O Lord God, be clothed with salvation, and let thy saints rejoice in goodness.
O Lord God, turn not away the face of thine anointed: remember the mercies of David thy servant.
